1338.title: Baba Bakala
1338.hook: where Makhan Shah found the ninth Guru
1338.howItsDone: Sikhs visit Gurdwara Baba Bakala Sahib and the place tradition remembers as Guru Tegh Bahadur's room of meditation, and they tell the story of Makhan Shah, especially around the ninth Guru's gurpurab.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tarn Taran, Guru Arjan's wide pool, and a look back down the week's road. Your line was a wide pool.

A man stands on a rooftop in a village, shouting to everyone below: the Guru is found! The Guru is found! Down in the lanes, people stop and look up, and a few of them are not happy to hear it. The village is Bakala, near the Beas. The man on the roof is a trader named Makhan Shah. And the one he found was not the loudest man in the village. He was the one sitting quietly.
screen: `A MAN ON A ROOFTOP.` → `THE GURU IS FOUND!` → `NOT THE LOUDEST. THE QUIET ONE.`

segments.voice: First, a riddle of two words. Tradition says the child Guru, Guru Har Krishan, as he was dying in Delhi, was asked who would come after him. He answered only: Baba Bakale. The Baba is in Bakala. Second, the crowd. When word spread, tradition says, many men in Bakala set up seats and called themselves the Guru, each with his own followers and his own claims. It was noisy, and it was confusing. Third, the test. This path has met Makhan Shah before, as a trader. Tradition says that in a storm at sea he had promised an offering to the Guru if his ship came through. In Bakala he didn't know whom to give it to, so he went from seat to seat, leaving each claimant a small gift and saying nothing of his promise. They took it, and thanked him. Then he came to Tegh Bahadur, a man who, tradition says, spent long hours in quiet meditation in a small room below ground. And Tegh Bahadur reminded him of the full promise he had made. That's when Makhan Shah ran up to the roof. Fourth, the teaching underneath. Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, later wrote hymns that are in the Guru Granth Sahib. In one, he says, in paraphrase: holy people, give up the pride of the mind. The one who was found had not been looking to be found. Today a gurdwara stands at Baba Bakala, and Sikhs visit the place tradition remembers as that underground room.

1339.title: Kiratpur Sahib
1339.hook: many Sikhs immerse the ashes of the dead in the river here
1339.howItsDone: After a cremation, Sikh families often bring the ashes to Gurdwara Patalpuri Sahib at Kiratpur, say the Ardas, and place them in the Sutlej; others use any nearby flowing water, as the Rehat Maryada allows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Baba Bakala, the rooftop, and the quiet one who was found. Your line was the guru found.

Nobody in the car says much on the long drive. In someone's lap sits a small bundle wrapped in white cloth. At the end of the road there's a river, the Sutlej, running fast and gray-green past a gurdwara on its bank. A family walks down to the water together, stands for a prayer, and lets the ashes go. The current takes them at once. This is Kiratpur Sahib, and Sikh families come here from near and far to do exactly this.
screen: `A QUIET DRIVE, A WHITE BUNDLE.` → `A FAST RIVER, A GURDWARA.` → `THE CURRENT TAKES THEM.`

segments.voice: First, the town. Kiratpur, on the Sutlej, is linked in tradition with Guru Hargobind, the sixth Guru, who spent his later years here: a town of the Gurus' families and memories. Second, the river gurdwara. Gurdwara Patalpuri Sahib stands on the bank, where Sikh families bring the ashes of the people they love, say the Ardas, and place them in the flowing water. Third, what Sikh teaching says, and doesn't. The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, says, in paraphrase, that after cremation the ashes may be put into any flowing water nearby, and it discourages building monuments over them. So no single place is required. Kiratpur isn't a rule. It's a choice made out of love, because the Gurus' own memory is close by. Fourth, the hymn. At night, and at the time of a funeral, Sikhs sing the Kirtan Sohila. In it Guru Nanak pictures death as a wedding day, in paraphrase: the day of the wedding is written; come, friends, pour oil on the threshold; give me your blessings, that I may meet my Lord. The house is full of people getting a bride ready to go. That's how the hymn sees the last leaving: not an end, but someone going home to the beloved. So at the riverbank, a family can grieve, and still hear the wedding song. Both are allowed.

1340.title: Hemkunt Sahib
1340.hook: a high Himalayan lake linked by tradition to the Tenth Guru's former life
1340.howItsDone: When the snow clears, Sikh pilgrims climb the steep trail to Hemkunt Sahib, bathe in the cold lake, and join the Ardas and kirtan at the gurdwara on its shore.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kiratpur Sahib on the Sutlej, and the Sohila's wedding song. Your line was ashes to the river.

For part of every year, snow closes the path. When it opens, pilgrims climb on foot or on ponies, up a steep trail in the Himalayas, past waterfalls and wildflowers, breathing hard in the thin air. At the top there's a lake, clear and very cold, ringed by peaks, and on its shore a gurdwara. Some pilgrims step into that icy water. The place is called Hemkunt Sahib, and Sikh tradition ties it to a life before the Tenth Guru's life.
screen: `SNOW CLOSES THE PATH.` → `A STEEP CLIMB, THIN AIR.` → `A COLD LAKE, A GURDWARA.`

segments.voice: First, the text. In the Bachittar Natak, a work in the Dasam Granth that Sikh tradition attributes to Guru Gobind Singh, the poet tells his own story. In paraphrase: in an earlier life, he did deep austerity on a mountain called Hemkunt, a place of peaks, absorbed in God, until God called him to be born into the world and spread the right way of living. He did not want to come, his mind was so joined to God's feet, but God sent him. Second, the finding. The poem names Hemkunt but gives no map. Long after the Guru, Sikhs identified this Himalayan lake as the Hemkunt of the poem, and a gurdwara was built on its shore. Third, the honest part. Sikhs hold different views here. Some read the passage as the Guru's literal memory of a former life; some read it as poetry about a calling. Some Sikhs also discuss which parts of the Dasam Granth are the Guru's own. This path describes these views; it doesn't decide. Fourth, what the pilgrims do with it. Whatever they think of the map, they climb a hard trail anyway. At the top, the poem's picture becomes something you can stand in: a still place, high up, close to the sky, where someone, tradition says, was so happy with God that he didn't want to leave. And left anyway, because he was sent.

segments.voice: See the water, very still and clear, the color of the sky, with white-topped peaks all around, and let the cold, thin air slow your breath on its own. Sit at the edge with nothing to do. Then remember the poem, someone happy in a place like this, called down into the busy world, and let your breath carry a little of the stillness down with you.

1341.title: Gurdwaras abroad
1341.hook: great gurdwaras stand in London, Toronto, Nairobi, Kuala Lumpur
1341.howItsDone: Sikhs around the world gather at local gurdwaras, where the Guru Granth Sahib is installed, kirtan is sung, and the langar serves a free meal to anyone who comes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hemkunt Sahib, the cold lake and the poem of a calling. Your line was the high lake.

Where does a Guru live when the family moves across the world? Try a wet London street, buses going by, and then a building with a dome and a tall saffron flag out front. A wide suburban road outside Toronto, a parking lot full on a Sunday morning. A gurdwara in Nairobi, its doors open to the morning traffic. One in Kuala Lumpur, shoes lined up at the door in the heat. Different weather, different streets, and inside each one the same thing at the center: the Guru Granth Sahib, on a raised seat, under a canopy.
screen: `LONDON, TORONTO.` → `NAIROBI, KUALA LUMPUR.` → `THE SAME THING AT THE CENTER.`

segments.voice: First, what makes a gurdwara. It isn't the dome or the city. Sikhs say the Guru Granth Sahib is the Guru, so wherever it is installed with respect, on a raised seat, opened each morning and put to rest at night, that place is the Guru's court, the darbar. A gurdwara in Toronto is not a copy of one in Punjab. It's the same Guru, in a new place. Second, the Guru's word on this. Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru, writes, in paraphrase: wherever my True Guru goes and sits, that place is beautiful. Some Sikhs far from Punjab hear their own story in that line. The Guru goes where the sangat goes. Third, two signs you can spot from the street. The Nishan Sahib, the tall flag, marks a gurdwara from a distance. The langar marks it from inside: a free kitchen where anyone may sit and eat, Sikh or not. Those two travel well. Fourth, what else grew in these buildings. For families who moved far from home, the gurdwara became more than a place to pray. It's where weddings happen, where children learn Gurmukhi letters on weekends, where newcomers find someone who speaks their language, and where a stranger can get a hot meal. In London, Toronto, Nairobi and Kuala Lumpur the details differ: the food, the accents, the weather at the door. The seat at the center is the same.

1342.title: The rababis
1342.hook: Muslim musicians descended from Mardana's tradition sang the Gurus' hymns at the Harmandir for generations
1342.howItsDone: Kirtan in gurdwaras is usually led by Sikh raagis today; a small number of musicians, Sikh and Muslim, keep rabab playing and the rababi way of singing alive in performance and recordings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gurdwaras abroad: London, Toronto, Nairobi, and the same Guru at the center. Your line was the guru abroad.

A wooden instrument with a rounded belly, a skin face, and strings that buzz low under a singing voice. That's a rabab. In the janamsakhi stories, Guru Nanak sings and a Muslim companion named Mardana plays a rabab beside him, village after village, road after road. This path first met him on day thirty-one. Tradition says Mardana's music didn't end with Mardana. Families of Muslim musicians kept the craft, and for generations they sang the Gurus' hymns at the Harmandir in Amritsar, until the partition of Punjab drew a border through their lives. Those singers have a name, and it's today's word.
screen: `A RABAB: SKIN, WOOD, LOW STRINGS.` → `MARDANA PLAYS; THE GURU SINGS.` → `THE MUSIC PASSED DOWN.`

segments.voice: First, the name. A rababi is simply a rabab player, and the word became the name for these families of Muslim kirtan singers. They sang Sikh scripture in the ragas it's written in, a calling passed from parent to child. Second, a place inside the book. The Guru Granth Sahib holds a ballad credited to two minstrels, Satta and Balwand, in Raag Ramkali, praising the Gurus and the light passing from one Guru to the next. Tradition remembers them as musicians at the Gurus' court. So some of the musicians' own words sit inside the scripture, sung in gurdwaras today. Third, what the border did. As rababi families remember it, when Punjab was divided they went west, to the new Pakistan, and the music they had carried into the Harmandir went with them. Their kind of kirtan was heard less and less on the Amritsar side. Some Sikhs speak of that as a real loss, and some musicians, Sikh and Muslim, have worked to bring the rabab back into kirtan. Fourth, the shape of the whole story. A Guru walks the roads with a Muslim friend and an instrument. The friend's heirs, Muslims too, keep singing the Guru's words for generations at the Harmandir. Nobody in that story had to stop being who they were to sing together: a faith whose hymns, in its own stories, were carried on a Muslim musician's strings.

1343.title: Raga or popular tune
1343.hook: some sing kirtan strictly in ragas, others in simpler tunes; both are loved
1343.howItsDone: Some gurdwaras and kirtan schools sing hymns in the ragas named in the Guru Granth Sahib; others use simpler tunes so the whole sangat can join, and some sangats hear both.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rababis, Muslim families who sang the Gurus' hymns on the rabab. Your line was mardana's heirs.

Two gurdwaras, a few streets apart, on the same evening. In the first, a raagi with a harmonium and a tabla player opens a hymn slowly, notes rising in a set order, a mood held a long while before the words begin. In the second, teenagers sing the same hymn to a simple tune you could hum after one hearing, and the whole hall sings back. Both are kirtan. Both are the Gurus' words. So which way is right? Sikhs have argued about it with real care, and that's today's question: raga or popular tune.
screen: `SAME HYMN, TWO HALLS.` → `A SLOW RAGA. A SIMPLE TUNE.` → `WHICH WAY IS RIGHT?`

segments.voice: First, the book itself is built on ragas. Open the Guru Granth Sahib and the hymns are gathered under raga headings: Sri Raag, Majh, Gauri, Asa, and on through the book. A raga is more than a scale: a set of notes, a way of moving between them, and a mood the music carries. So some Sikhs say plainly: if a Guru set a hymn in a raga, sing it in that raga. The music is part of the message, and changing it loses something the Guru chose. Second, the other side. Others say what matters is that the words reach people. A simple tune lets a whole hall sing, a child learn a hymn by heart on the way home, a newcomer join on the very first night. For them, a tune that opens the door is doing the Guru's work. Third, what the scripture says about ragas themselves. In a var in Sri Raag, Guru Amar Das names Sri Raag as the finest of the ragas, and adds the condition in the same breath. In paraphrase: it is finest if, through it, a person holds love for the truth. Even the praise of a raga is tied to love. Fourth, both are loved. Some gurdwaras keep strict raga kirtan; others sing simpler tunes; some sangats hear both in one week. Those who keep the ragas guard something precious. Those who sing simply open a door. The line from Sri Raag sits over both: the music serves the love, not the other way around.

1344.title: The dhadis
1344.hook: ballad-singers with small drums and a fiddle sing the panth's history
1344.howItsDone: Dhadi jathas sing vars and ballads of Sikh history with the dhad and sarangi at gurdwaras and gatherings, mixing sung verse with spoken narration, especially on days that remember martyrs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, raga or popular tune: two ways to sing one hymn. Your line was both are loved.

Halfway through the song, the singer stops singing and starts talking. A Guru on the move, a martyr who wouldn't bend, a battle at a river: the story comes out plainly, and the crowd leans in. Then the drum comes back, a small hourglass drum held up in one hand and struck with the other, with a bowed fiddle crying along beside it, and the story turns into song again. The singers stand rather than sit, and their voices are built to carry across a crowded courtyard. These ballad-singers are today's word.
screen: `AN HOURGLASS DRUM. A FIDDLE.` → `THE SONG STOPS; THE STORY STARTS.` → `THEN THE DRUM AGAIN.`

segments.voice: First, the name. A dhadi is a ballad-singer who plays the dhad, that small hourglass drum, usually with a sarangi, the bowed fiddle, beside it. Second, a name a Guru took for himself. In a var in Raag Majh, Guru Nanak calls himself a dhadi. In paraphrase: I was a minstrel with no work, and the Lord put me to work, singing praise day and night. Not a king, not a judge, not a scholar: a wandering ballad-singer, glad to be hired. A humble trade became a Guru's picture of his own calling. Third, history sung. Tradition says Guru Hargobind welcomed dhadis to sing vars, ballads of courage, at the Akal Takht, the seat he raised facing the Harmandir. This path met the var back on day five hundred thirty-six. A var praises those who stood firm, so dhadis turned the panth's story into song: the Gurus, the martyrs, the battles, the families who paid a price. For anyone without a history book, the dhadi was one, out loud, with a drum. Fourth, the way it's done. Song and speech take turns. The singers give a verse; one steps out and tells the story plainly; the verse returns, and the crowd now knows why it matters. Dhadi jathas still sing at gurdwaras and gatherings, especially on days that remember martyrs.
